title: Builder Incentives vs Lender Incentives: How to Compare
description: How to compare builder incentives, from a rate buydown to a closing cost credit, with lender offers using the Loan Estimate and real numbers.
body:
New construction shoppers often see a headline offer: a closing cost credit, a lower rate for a set period, or both. A lender can also put its own offer on the table. The trouble is that these offers rarely look alike, so it is easy to compare the wrong things.

This post covers a plain way to line them up. It is general information, not lending or tax advice. A lender and the official sources below can speak to your exact situation.

## What the two kinds of incentives are

{{img:0}}

A builder incentive is something the builder offers as part of the sale. Common examples are a credit toward closing costs or money toward a rate buydown. A lender incentive comes from the lender, and it might be a lower fee, a different rate option, or a program for certain buyers.

Two terms come up a lot:

- **Closing cost credit:** money applied toward your closing costs. Closing costs typically run 2 to 4 percent of the purchase price, plus earnest money and moving costs.
- **Rate buydown:** money used to lower the interest rate, either for the first period of the loan (temporary) or for the life of the loan (permanent).

Buyers can ask a seller to pay some closing costs or to fund a temporary or permanent buydown. Whether that is available depends on the seller, the home and the market, and the lender must confirm what is allowed for your loan.

## Start with the Loan Estimate

The best tool for comparing is a document, not a sales sheet. After you apply, a lender must give you a Loan Estimate within three business days. It is a standard three-page form, so estimates from different lenders can be compared side by side.

The CFPB encourages borrowers to get Loan Estimates from more than one lender, because interest rates and fees can differ from lender to lender. You can read their plain-language guides at the CFPB Owning a Home guides.

A few practical points:

- You choose your own lender. You are free to use any lender you like, and that includes a different one than the lender a builder mentions.
- If an incentive depends on using a particular lender, ask for that condition in writing. Then get at least one other Loan Estimate to compare.
- Credit-scoring models generally treat several mortgage inquiries made within a short period as a single inquiry. Comparing lenders close together is usually less harmful than spreading applications out. Ask each lender how this works for you.
- Lenders include banks, credit unions, mortgage brokers and online lenders. A mortgage broker compares offers from several lenders on your behalf.

## Rate buydown or closing cost credit

{{img:1}}

These two can feel similar, since both are "money from the builder." They work differently.

A closing cost credit lowers the cash you bring to closing. It does not change your monthly payment. If your savings are stretched, that can matter.

A rate buydown lowers the payment. A temporary buydown does that for a limited period, and then the rate steps up. A permanent buydown lowers the rate for the loan term. The 30-year fixed mortgage rate was 7.40% for the week of 2026-10-08, according to Freddie Mac via FRED. You can see the current series at Freddie Mac 30-year mortgage rate (FRED). Nobody can reliably predict where rates will go, so treat any future refinance as a possibility, not a plan. A refinance depends on rates, credit, home value and income at that time, and it has closing costs of its own.

To see how a payment changes, try your own numbers in the [Mortgage calculator](/mortgage-calculator). Then ask the lender to show you the payment after any buydown period ends, not just during it.

## Compare the full cost, not just the incentive

An incentive is one line in a bigger picture. Before you decide, put these side by side for each option:

1. **The purchase price.** A credit on a higher price is not the same as a lower price. Ask how the incentive and the price relate.
2. **The interest rate and the APR on the Loan Estimate.** The form shows both.
3. **Cash to close.** Look at the total after credits.
4. **The monthly payment.** Include taxes, insurance and any mortgage insurance. Private mortgage insurance is typically required on conventional loans when the down payment is under 20 percent.
5. **Conditions and deadlines.** Does the incentive require a certain closing date, a certain loan type or a certain lender?
6. **What is in writing.** If it is not in the contract or a signed addendum, ask for it to be added.

Loan type can change the picture too. FHA loans allow a down payment as low as 3.5 percent. VA loans typically require no down payment and no monthly mortgage insurance, though a funding fee may apply. The [VA home loans](https://www.va.gov/housing-assistance/home-loans/) page and HUD buying a home explain the basics. The Tennessee Housing Development Agency offers home loan programs through participating lenders, so ask any lender you are considering whether they take part. You can learn more at [the Tennessee Housing Development Agency](https://www.thda.org).

## Local numbers to keep in mind

How much room there is to negotiate depends on local conditions, and those differ by city. Months of supply is how long it would take to sell every active listing at the current pace of sales. Under 4 months favors sellers, 4 to 6 months is balanced, and over 6 months favors buyers.

For the Nashville metro area, Redfin showed 5.4 months of supply for the 4 weeks ending 2026-09-27. For Spring Hill, Redfin showed 3.9 months of supply on a rolling 3-month basis as of 2026-08-31. Franklin was at 3.4 months on the same basis and date. These are area-wide numbers, and a single community or price range can look different. You can see more on the [Market data for the I-65 corridor](/market-data) page.

Also keep in mind that Spring Hill includes parts of both Williamson and Maury counties. Taxes, schools and county services can differ by address, so verify them with the school district and the county for any home you are serious about.

## Questions to ask before you sign

- What exactly is the incentive worth, and where is it written down?
- Does it depend on a lender, a loan type or a closing date?
- What is the rate and payment once any buydown period ends?
- How does the price compare with similar homes, with and without the incentive?
- What do the Loan Estimates from at least two lenders show?

When closing gets close, the lender must send the Closing Disclosure at least 3 business days before closing. Compare it with your Loan Estimate and ask about anything that changed.

## Want a second set of eyes?

If you are weighing a builder offer against another option, I am glad to walk through it with you. Fill out the form at [Get matched with homes](/buy#form) and I will schedule a call, and we will be talking within the next 48 hours. You can also reach me through [Contact Scott](/contact).

Scott Davis, REALTOR® with Hive Nashville

faq.q: What is the difference between a rate buydown and a closing cost credit?
faq.a: A closing cost credit lowers the cash you need at closing. A rate buydown uses money to lower your interest rate, either for a set period or for the life of the loan. A lender must confirm what is allowed for your loan.

faq.q: Do I have to use the builder's lender to get an incentive?
faq.a: You choose your own lender and are free to use any lender you like. If an incentive is tied to a certain lender, ask for the terms in writing and get a Loan Estimate from at least one other lender to compare.

faq.q: How do I compare lender offers side by side?
faq.a: Use the Loan Estimate. A lender must provide it within three business days after you apply, and it is a standard three-page form. The CFPB encourages getting Loan Estimates from more than one lender.

faq.q: How much are closing costs on a new home?
faq.a: Closing costs typically run 2 to 4 percent of the purchase price, plus earnest money and moving costs. Your Loan Estimate shows the figures for your loan.
